_comment: Single source of truth for the 11-week calendar. Transcribed from Curricula/Weeks/week1..11.png; weeks 1, 7 and 11 redistributed for holidays (decisions D-0015..D-0017). Every other path is derived as {week.dir}/{day.slug}. Calendar dates derive from startDate + week index + weekday slot (day 1=Mon..5=Fri); a slot whose date is in holidays is {day, kind: holiday} only. The weekly feedback form is the last teaching day of each week (derived, never hand-set). status: planned | authored | live (D-0052). The harness Wire step writes authored (every artifact exists and passed; the page is written but not linked from the index, which is what hides a week authored ahead) or live when the week has already started on --today (args_for.py releaseOnWire); harness/release_week.py flips authored->live on the Friday before the week and is the only other writer of live. demoFormat: py | nb | none | loose (none = concept day with no code demo; the runbook carries facilitation scripts, D-0030. loose = the trainer improvises; a plan ladder's scripts and keys are an optional fallback and harness/close_day.py publishes what was typed from the demo repo, D-0050). taught: YYYY-MM-DD, set ONLY by harness/close_day.py after the session; harness/publish_demos.py copies the answer keys from trainer/<rel>/demos/key/ to demos/<rel>/ only when it is set (D-0030).

exitCriteria._comment: D-0063: Revature's per-group exit criteria (Required / Preferred / Stretch rows), the mock-interview and exam bar when a group ends. Source of truth is the markdown drop zone sourceDir (one file per group, lowercase qc-N-<slug>.md; a group whose file is absent is 'not published yet'); harness/exit_criteria.py parses it at runtime, nothing is hand-maintained here. Ids are <group>.<section slug>.<tier letter><2-digit row within tier within section>, so a published group's file is append-only: never delete or reorder a row once its page is live. fromWeek: the first week whose plan must carry a complete '## Exit criteria map' (plan_check) and whose day authors and critics are bound by the rows; earlier weeks got a read-only backfill map and harness/plans/exit-audit-qc1.md.

weeks.theme: Agile for developers, Git & Python fundamentals
weeks.notes: WEEK ARC (D-0024): Tue = how software teams work (SDLC, Scrum, story pointing, Git as the team's workflow). Wed-Fri = Python the way a team writes it. Audience (D-0048): some programming in any language, no Python, Git, terminal or CS theory assumed, so: Wed assumes the Tue tooling check passed and teaches Python's syntax from first principles (blocks and indentation, variables and types, operators, print and input) together with the conventions a team expects (PEP 8, naming, comments that earn their place); Thu assumes Wed and teaches the data types, then their idioms and pitfalls; Fri assumes Thu and teaches control flow, functions and classes, then when to choose each (when a function, when a class, scope). Every notes page opens by naming in one sentence what it assumes from earlier days of this course and never claims the reader knows anything from outside it.

days.title: Orientation, Agile & Git fundamentals
days.subtitle: SDLC · Scrum · story pointing · git init/commit/branch/merge/push/pull
subtopics: Source control management (git, vcs, cvcs, dvcs)
days.notes: DAY SHAPE (D-0024): the first 30 minutes are an on-ramp, not a lesson: orientation (what/why Python, professionalism at Revature) and a tooling check (interpreter vs compiler, REPL, Jupyter, where Python sits in the full stack) explained briefly from first principles (D-0048: none of it is assumed), enough to confirm the setup works and nothing more. The day's real content is how software teams work: SDLC -> Agile vs waterfall -> Scrum -> story pointing -> Git as the team's workflow -> Git exercise. Notes page: at most ONE step on the on-ramp, every other step on team practice; do not teach Python syntax or pytest (that is Wed-Fri). Demos: at most one on the on-ramp. EXERCISE (D-0025, exerciseKind rubric): the Git exercise IS the exercise: a real repository on GitHub with a feature branch, a merge, one resolved conflict and well-written commit messages, marked against a rubric. No pytest, no starter module.

days.notes: DAY SHAPE (D-0054): two headlines, testing and NumPy. The morning teaches testing on the desk's own rules (overview, unit testing, pytest); the afternoon teaches NumPy as a library of its own, against W1D4's lists: an array of ticket resolution hours where a list was, with the vectorised arithmetic, dtype and shape differences shown and then tested with pytest. NumPy gets at least two notes steps and at least one demo rung of its own; it is never a mention inside the testing steps. Interview mindset part 1 is a facilitation block, not a demo.

The morning teaches Counter, namedtuple and OrderedDict on the ticket records; the afternoon teaches pandas as a library of its own, against the morning's Counter and namedtuple and Tuesday's JSON files: a DataFrame of tickets loaded from the desk's JSON file, grouped and counted where Counter was, columns where namedtuple fields were. pandas gets at least two notes steps and at least one demo rung of its own; it is never a mention inside the collections steps.

days.title: Review, Matplotlib & mini-project
days.subtitle: data visualisation · Matplotlib · Python review · mini-project
days.notes: DAY SHAPE (D-0054): Matplotlib is a headline of the day, taught against Thursday's DataFrame: the overview of data visualisation first, then a Matplotlib chart of tickets per status drawn from the DataFrame, saved to a file. Matplotlib gets at least two notes steps and at least one demo rung of its own; it is never a mention inside the review. The Python review is the rest of the day: a recap of weeks 1-2 folded into a rubric mini-project (exerciseKind rubric, D-0025) that uses the week's modules, JSON file, tests, arrays, DataFrame and chart; no pytest starter module.

weeks.notes: WEEK ARC (D-0054): the week turns last week's single-file ticket desk into a small professional codebase, one library at a time, each library a headline of its own day. Audience (D-0048): some programming in any language, no Python, Git, terminal or CS theory beyond what week 1 taught, so: Mon assumes W1D5's functions and classes and teaches modules and packaging from first principles (import, the math module, logging, regex, pip and installing a package, pylint, then splitting the desk into a module of its own); Tue assumes Mon's modules and teaches errors and exception handling, then file handling (read, write and create, delete) and JSON as the file format the desk saves tickets in; Wed assumes Tue's JSON-backed desk and teaches testing (overview, unit testing, pytest) against the desk's rules, then NumPy taught against W1D4's lists: an array of resolution hours where a list was, with the difference shown and tested; Thu assumes Wed's tests and arrays and teaches the collections module (Counter, namedtuple, OrderedDict) on the ticket records, then pandas taught against Thu's Counter and namedtuple and Tue's JSON files: a DataFrame of tickets loaded from the JSON file, grouped and counted where Counter was; Fri assumes Thu's DataFrame and teaches data visualisation (overview, then Matplotlib charting the DataFrame as tickets per status), then a Python review folded into a rubric mini-project. NumPy, pandas and Matplotlib each get their own notes steps and their own demo rungs, never a mention inside another library's step. Every notes page opens by naming in one sentence what it assumes from earlier days of this course and never claims the reader knows anything from outside it.

WEEK ARC (D-0059): the week moves the ticket desk's records out of tickets.json into MySQL tables. MySQL 9.7 runs in a Docker container on every laptop (image tag mysql:9.7 floats within the LTS line: 9.7.4 on 2026-10-22; name the tag, never a patch version) (image mysql:9.7, the LTS line; `docker run --name desk-mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=... -p 3306:3306 -v desk-data:/var/lib/mysql -d mysql:9.7`), and the mysql client is reached through `docker exec -it desk-mysql mysql -uroot -p`; Docker Desktop is installed before Monday (announced on W2D5, re-checked in Monday's setup step). Audience (D-0048): some programming in any language plus what weeks 1 and 2 taught, no SQL and no Docker, so: Mon assumes W2D5's desk and teaches Docker from first principles in its setup step (image, container, volume, port, the client inside the container) and then what a relational database is, tables, data types and modelling the desk's tickets, customers and agents as an ERD before any CREATE TABLE; Tue assumes Mon's schema and teaches the sublanguages (DDL, DML, DQL, DCL, TCL) on those tables in the mysql client; Wed assumes Tue's rows and teaches keys, constraints and normalisation by rebuilding the schema properly, then from Wednesday on Python reaches the database through mysql-connector-python 26.7.0 (pure-Python wheel on 3.15) so the desk's storage module writes to MySQL where it wrote JSON; Thu assumes Wed's constrained schema and teaches clauses, functions, joins and subqueries in the client, then transactions (ACID, commit, rollback, isolation) with ticket assignment as the transaction the Python desk runs; Fri assumes Thu's joins and transactions and teaches triggers, views, stored procedures, user-defined functions and indexes on the desk's tables, then a review. Mon and Tue are SQL in the client only; Wed to Fri alternate SQL in the client and the Python desk, never both in one block. Every notes page opens by naming in one sentence what it assumes from earlier days of this course and never claims the reader knows anything from outside it.
